name: Customer 360 / CDP
description: A customer 360 stitches every trace of a customer — product events, CRM records, transactions, support tickets — into one profile: event collection lands the raw signals, identity resolution matches them across systems (deterministic keys first, probabilistic matching for the rest), and a profile store maintains golden records with computed traits. Segmentation builds audiences on those profiles and activation syncs them to ad platforms, email, and the product itself. The modern build is the composable CDP: profiles live in your warehouse with resolution and activation as tools on top, rather than in a vendor's black box. Consent enforcement is not a feature here — it is the architecture's license to operate.
when_to_use: Customer data is fragmented across product, CRM, billing, and support, and nobody can answer 'what happened with this customer?'
Marketing and product teams need segments built on complete profiles, synced automatically to every destination.
Personalization requires knowing the same person across anonymous web visits, logged-in product use, and offline purchases.
You already have a warehouse and want a composable CDP on it rather than shipping customer data into another vendor silo.
when_not_to_use: One system already holds effectively all customer data — resolution machinery without fragmentation is pure cost.
The need is governed master data for operations and compliance rather than marketing activation — that is the MDM hub (17).
Consent and privacy operations are immature — activating unified profiles without enforceable consent is a regulatory incident in waiting.
Only aggregate analytics is needed — a warehouse with BI (2) answers 'how many customers' without per-person profiles.

hot_spots.title: Identity overreach
hot_spots.detail: Aggressive probabilistic matching merges two real people into one profile — and the wrong person gets the email, the price, or the data export.

hot_spots.title: Consent drift
hot_spots.detail: Audiences activate faster than consent flags propagate; a suppressed customer receiving one campaign is a reportable incident in many regimes.

hot_spots.title: Stale traits
hot_spots.detail: Batch-computed traits activate yesterday's behavior — churn campaigns fire at customers who already renewed.

hot_spots.title: Destination divergence
hot_spots.detail: Each ad and email platform re-interprets audience definitions slightly differently, so 'the same segment' differs per channel.

evolution.reason: Graduate customer identity into governed master data when operations and compliance need it beyond marketing.

stages.name: Event collection
stages.role: SDKs and pipelines landing behavioral and system data with identifiers intact
stages.rationale: Segment defined the collection-SDK category; RudderStack is the warehouse-native open alternative that keeps raw events in your own store.

stages.name: Identity resolution
stages.role: Matching identities across systems into a persistent person graph
stages.rationale: Zingg runs ML-based matching on Spark inside your own platform; suite CDPs and MDM tools bundle resolution when you buy rather than build.

stages.name: Profile store
stages.role: Golden customer records and computed traits, queryable at scale
stages.rationale: The composable pattern keeps profiles in the warehouse you already govern; Redis fronts it only when the product needs sub-millisecond profile lookups.

stages.name: Segmentation + activation
stages.role: Audience definitions synced continuously to ads, email, and product
stages.rationale: Reverse-ETL tools turn warehouse audiences into destination syncs with per-destination field mapping — the activation half of a composable CDP.

stages.name: Consent + privacy
stages.role: Purpose, opt-out, and suppression enforcement on every activation path
stages.rationale: Consent must gate activation structurally — a privacy platform managing purposes and suppressions is what makes the CDP legally operable.
